title: KV hotset skew, eviction tuning, and memory-bandwidth notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a working note capturing our latest experiments exploring how hotset skew and eviction heuristics interact with paging and memory bandwidth on GPU-backed serving nodes. Goal is to find actionable tuning knobs that lower 95/99p token tail latency while keeping steady-state token cost low.

High level summary (TL;DR):
- Workloads with high Zipf skew (alpha >= 1.1) show a small hotset (~1-3% of cache entries) driving ~60-80% of reuse. When hotset is undersized, eviction churn causes upstream paging and large memcpy traffic to/from device, increasing p95 token latency by ~25-40%.
- LRU alone under high skew evicts frequently accessed cold entries when hotset size < ~3%, causing visible reuse-rate oscillation. A small LFU component or a pinned hotset reduces churn and lowers tail latency.
- Paging (host<->GPU) bandwidth becomes the bottleneck when active working set > GPU DRAM * 0.85; measured sustained copy rates hit 36-44 GB/s on our A40 nodes during thrash windows. Avoiding synchronous page-in on critical fast-path reduces latency spikes.

Bench setup notes:
- Cluster: 4x A40 (48 GB) per node, driver 525, CUDA 12.2, Ubuntu 22.04. Serving runtime from branch: feature/kv-evict-tuning-2025.
- Workload generator: local synthetic trace harness (zipf generator) + replay traces from conversation logs (sampled prod session ids).
- Prompts: mix of short (32 tokens), medium (128 tokens), and long (512 tokens). Under long prompts we see larger KV trace reuse due to longer KV cache lifetimes.
- Metrics collected: per-request KV hits, reuse_distance histogram (log-bucketed), eviction rate (/s), bytes_copied_host_gpu (/s), GPU memcpy latency histogram, p50/p95/p99 token latency, CPU steal/blocked cycles. Tools: nsight-cu, nvtx annotations, bpftrace scripts (attached in linked artifacts), perf counters.

Experiments run (index):
1) Hotset sizing sweep (zipf alpha 1.0/1.1/1.2, hotset reserve 0.5%..8%).
   - Findings: alpha 1.2 => hotset 2.5% captured ~75% reuse. Setting reserve to 4% gave marginal +6% hit rate but reduced eviction churn by ~40%.
   - Notes: diminishing returns after 6% reserve; memory pressure growth outweighs hit gains.

2) Eviction policy: LRU vs seg-LRU (2-segment) vs LRU+LFU decay (freq window 10k ops).
   - Results: seg-LRU reduced repeated evictions of the hottest entries by >50% vs plain LRU. LRU+LFU delivered the best steady reuse under skewed traces (hit rate +4-6%), but LFU window tuning is sensitive and can over-promote stale heavy hitters under bursty writes.

3) Eviction granularity: entry-based vs chunked (64KB/256KB).
   - Observations: chunked eviction reduced bookkeeping overhead but increased overfetch on some models where entries are small (<1KB). 64KB chunk struck a good balance; 256KB caused extra memory moves and worsened p99 by +8ms in some runs.

4) Async prefetch + background warming vs sync page-in:
   - Async prefetch (predict next token KV pages from sequence context) reduced p95 by ~12% when hotset hit-rate near threshold. Background warming prevented synchronous host<->GPU memcpy on critical path.

Profiling snippets (representative):
- reuse_distance distribution (alpha=1.1, hotset reserve=2%):
  bucket < 10: 62%
  10-100: 18%
  100-1k: 10%
  >1k: 10%
- eviction churn trace (LRU, undersized hotset): repeated evictions of same key within 3s window = 15% of total evictions.
- memory bandwidth snapshot (during thrash): nvprof shows device->host copies 22 GB/s, host->device 18 GB/s sustained, peaks 44 GB/s (short).
- CPU: 6-12% time waiting on memcpy (observed via nvtx ranges) during worst windows.

Key hypotheses validated/invalidated:
- Hypothesis A (validated): small pinned hotset reduces repeated evictions and improves tail latency under skewed access.
- Hypothesis B (partially validated): eviction granularity affects memcpy overhead; but optimal granularity is model/entry-size dependent. No single global chunk works for all models.
- Hypothesis C (invalidated): simply increasing total cache size by 10% always improves p99. In several runs increased cache size pushed us into memory pressure that triggered paging thresholds and made p99 worse. So intelligent pinning wins over brute force size increases.

Actionable tuning recommendations (near-term):
- Introduce "hotset-reserve" config (percent of entries) default 3% for production tier with skew detection. Auto-scale reserve by observing reuse_concentration (e.g., fraction of hits in top 5% keys).
- Use seg-LRU by default; provide opt-in LRU+LFU for read-heavy workloads with stable distributions.
- Eviction granularity: default 64KB, but expose per-model override and provide a quick heuristic (median entry size * 8).
- Make page-in on critical path async with background priority prefetch. If async prefetch misses, fall back to synchronous but record metric.
- Add a memory-pressure soft-threshold at 80% DRAM usage on GPU to trigger conservative eviction aggressiveness before paging.

Operational signals to surface in Console:
- Hotset reuse concentration metric (top-k hit fraction) with alerts when concentration drops rapidly (indicates workload shift).
- Eviction churn rate and repeated-evict-of-same-key ratio.
- Host<->GPU memcpy bytes/s and peak copy bursts per minute.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Can we detect and automatically pin ephemeral ephemeral hotsets for short-lived bursts (e.g., a viral prompt pattern) without long-term promotion? Experiment: ephemeral pin TTL 30s vs 300s.
- Evaluate hybrid persistence: keep small cold-index on device that can store compressed pointers to full entries on host to avoid full page copies; measure CPU overhead vs memcpy savings.
- Test behavior under mixed-tenancy with noisy neighbors; results above are single-customer runs. We should run cross-tenant traces to see eviction fairness issues.

Debug checklist (for reproducing a bad window):
- grab nvtx logs for serving-runtime (last 10 minutes)
- collect reuse_distance histogram and top-100 keys by access time
- dump eviction-events with timestamps and sizes
- record GPU DRAM usage and host swap activity (if any)
- don't forget to include client trace id so we can correlate input distribution

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Add microbench for chunked eviction on entries <1KB (Ravi).
- Hook up Console alert POC for 'eviction-churn' (Aisha).
- Run multi-tenant stress harness with 1:10 hotset skew variation (Sofia).
- Draft short runbook for oncall: when memcpy bytes/s > 30 GB/s and p95 > target, flip to conservative policy.

Misc references / quick commands:
- bpftrace one-liner we used to count page-related syscalls: sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_madvise /comm=="serving-runtime"/ { @[comm] = count(); }'
- nvprof/NSIGHT: record memcpy ranges around NVTX "kv-page-in" markers to get precise copy durations.

Appendix: sample diff evidence (from run 2026-02-18):
- baseline (LRU, reserve=1%): p95 token latency = 36.2ms, hit rate 72%, repeated-evict ratio 0.18, memcpy peak 42 GB/s.
- tuned (seg-LRU, reserve=4%, async prefetch): p95 token latency = 26.9ms, hit rate 78%, repeated-evict ratio 0.07, memcpy peak 24 GB/s.

If anyone is reproducing, start from branch feature/kv-evict-tuning-2025, synth trace zipf-alpha 1.1, and run collectors enabled. Logs in s3://redwood-internal/kv-hotset-experiments/2026-02-18/.

-- Marcus
